newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco's traders want sugar price control lifted.
newsitem.headline: Morocco's traders want sugar price control lifted.

text.p: Morocco's sugar traders have urged the government to issue new measures to consolidate the commodity liberalisation by lifting control over sugar wholesale prices, a spokesman said on Monday.
The government has been gradually liberalising commodity imports since May 1996 to comply with World Trade Organisation rules but kept tight control on the market prices.

"Sugar traders and professionals of the sector support the government's commodity liberalisation process...But we hope that measures to accompany this policy can be issued and a three-year transition period set up before a full market liberalisation," Haddadi Louazani, head of the Professional Sugar Association, told Reuters.
According to Louzani, sugar farmers who play a vital role in provinding the market with nearly 50 percent of sugar needs also became hostages of the liberalisation policy.
The association said "competitive prices" on the world market were threatening farmers efforts and the local industry as a whole.
"We want a flexibility for the price fixing of farm produce and finished products," Louzani added.
A Casablanca-based market analyst said the sugar traders' reaction followed a government decision to delay a rise of sugar and edible oil wholesale prices expected for mid-March.

An official at the trade ministry said earlier there was "an agreement of principle" for a price increase. But, he said, this was under special conditions related to many factors including social issues. He gave no other details.

The government subsidises imported edible oil and sugar at an average of 5,000 dirhams ($532) and 2,000 ($213) per tonne respectively, the trade ministry said. It also maintains control over selling prices to avoid shortages and speculation on the domestic market, the ministry added.
"To be effective, the liberalisation should go until the end of its logical development," the sugar association said but did not elaborate.
Morocco has 13 sugar plants which refine a total of 3.5 million tonnes of sugar beet and 1.2 million tonnes of sugar cane annually.
"This quantity represents nearly half of the country's sugar consumption which grows by an average 3.0 percent every year," the association said.
Morocco's sugar consumption per capita was estimated at 33 kgs (82.5 lb) per head in 1996, it added.
According to the Office des Changes bureau, Morocco imported 512,613 tonnes of raw sugar at a cost of 1.34 billion dirhams ($164 million) from January to December 1996, most of it from South America.
